# Biochemistry

> Biomolecules and an overview of metabolic pathways — shared with chemistry.

## Molecules of life

Carbohydrates, lipids, proteins and nucleic acids each have structures suiting their roles. This connects directly to chemistry's biomolecules topic.

## Metabolism

Metabolic pathways are linked reactions building (anabolism) or breaking down (catabolism) molecules, controlled by enzymes, releasing or storing energy.

## What you should be able to do

- Describe major biomolecules
- Outline metabolism
- Relate structure to function

biology.A1.cell-biology-depth.subject: biology

biology.A1.cell-biology-depth.summary: Membrane transport, the cell cycle, and cell division (mitosis and meiosis).
biology.A1.cell-biology-depth.notes:
# Cell Biology at Depth

> Membrane transport, the cell cycle, and cell division (mitosis and meiosis).

## Cell cycle and division

Cells grow and divide in a controlled cycle. Mitosis makes two identical cells (growth, repair); meiosis makes four genetically varied gametes (reproduction).

## Why meiosis matters

Meiosis halves the chromosome number and shuffles genes, creating the variation that Genetics I described. It is the molecular source of inherited diversity.

## What you should be able to do

- Detail membrane transport
- Describe the cell cycle
- Compare mitosis and meiosis

---

biology.A1.molecular-genetics.summary: Transcription, translation and gene regulation in detail.
biology.A1.molecular-genetics.notes:
# Molecular Genetics

> Transcription, translation and gene regulation in detail.

## Gene expression

Transcription copies a gene to mRNA; translation reads mRNA codons (three bases) to build a protein from amino acids. The genetic code maps codons to amino acids.

## Regulation

Cells switch genes on and off so the right proteins are made at the right time — why a nerve cell and a skin cell differ despite identical DNA.

## What you should be able to do

- Detail transcription and translation
- Explain the genetic code
- Describe gene regulation

---

biology.A2.evolution-depth.notes:
# Evolution at Depth

> Speciation, molecular evidence and phylogenetics.

## Speciation

New species form when populations become reproductively isolated and diverge — often by geographic separation. This explains life's branching diversity.

## Molecular phylogenetics

Comparing DNA sequences reconstructs evolutionary relationships as trees. More similar sequences mean more recent common ancestors.

## What you should be able to do

- Explain speciation
- Use molecular evidence
- Read phylogenetic trees

---

biology.A2.genetics-ii.notes:
# Genetics II

> Linkage, mutation, genetic disorders and population genetics (Hardy-Weinberg).

## Beyond simple inheritance

Genes on the same chromosome are linked; mutations change DNA, sometimes causing disorders. Real inheritance is richer than single-gene ratios.

## Population genetics

Hardy-Weinberg predicts allele frequencies in a stable population — reusing probability and algebra to study evolution quantitatively.

## What you should be able to do

- Explain linkage and mutation
- Analyse genetic disorders
- Apply Hardy-Weinberg

---

biology.F1.the-cell.notes:
# The Cell

> Cell theory, cell structure, and the differences between plant and animal cells.

## Cell theory

All living things are made of cells; the cell is the basic unit of life; cells come from pre-existing cells. This unifying model underlies all of biology.

## Structure and function

Organelles have jobs: the nucleus controls, mitochondria release energy, chloroplasts (plants) capture light. Plant cells add a wall, chloroplasts and a large vacuole.

## What you should be able to do

- State cell theory
- Identify cell structures
- Compare plant and animal cells

---

biology.F2.reproduction.notes:
# Reproduction

> Asexual and sexual reproduction, and the human reproductive system.

## Two strategies

Asexual reproduction makes identical offspring from one parent (fast, no variation). Sexual reproduction combines two parents' genes, producing variation — the raw material for evolution.

## Human reproduction

Sexual reproduction in humans joins sperm and egg; the resulting variation is why siblings differ. This links directly to later genetics.

## What you should be able to do

- Compare asexual and sexual reproduction

- Explain variation from sexual reproduction

# Cell Processes

> Diffusion, osmosis and active transport — how substances cross membranes.

## Passive movement

Diffusion moves particles from high to low concentration; osmosis is the diffusion of water across a membrane. Both are passive — no energy needed.

## Active transport

Moving substances against a concentration gradient needs energy (active transport). Cells use it to absorb nutrients even when scarce.

## What you should be able to do

- Explain diffusion and osmosis
- Describe active transport
- Relate transport to concentration

# Ecology & Ecosystems

> Energy pyramids, nutrient cycles and population basics.

## Energy pyramids

Energy decreases up trophic levels (only ~10% passes on), so top predators are few. This explains pyramid shapes and short food chains.

## Cycles

Matter (carbon, nitrogen, water) cycles through ecosystems, unlike energy which flows through and is lost. Decomposers return nutrients to the soil.

## What you should be able to do

- Explain population change

# Enzymes

> Enzymes as biological catalysts, and the factors that affect their activity.

## Biological catalysts

Enzymes speed up reactions by lowering activation energy, binding substrates at an active site (lock-and-key). They are not used up — reusing the catalyst idea from chemistry.

## Sensitive to conditions

Temperature and pH affect enzyme shape; too much denatures them permanently. Each enzyme has an optimum, explaining why body temperature matters.

## What you should be able to do

- Describe factors affecting enzymes
- Relate enzymes to reaction rate

## Natural selection

Individuals vary; those better suited to the environment survive and reproduce more, passing on their traits. Over generations, populations adapt.

Evolution explains the diversity and relatedness of life. Evidence comes from fossils, anatomy, and DNA — a single framework for all biology.

biology.I2.population-biology.notes:
# Population Biology

> Exponential and logistic growth, and what limits populations.

## Growth models

Unchecked populations grow exponentially; real ones level off (logistic) as resources limit them at the carrying capacity — reusing exponentials from maths.

## Limiting factors

Food, space, predators and disease limit growth. Understanding them predicts population dynamics and informs conservation.

## What you should be able to do

- Model population growth
- Explain limiting factors
- Use exponential/logistic ideas

chemistry.A1.chemical-equilibrium.notes:
# Chemical Equilibrium (Quantitative)

> Equilibrium constants Kc and Kp, and ICE-table calculations.

## Equilibrium constant

Kc expresses the ratio of product to reactant concentrations at equilibrium (each raised to its coefficient). A large K favours products.

## ICE tables

Initial–Change–Equilibrium tables organise the algebra of finding equilibrium concentrations — systematic problem-solving reusing algebra skills.

## What you should be able to do

- Write equilibrium expressions
- Use Kc and Kp
- Solve with ICE tables

chemistry.A1.chemical-kinetics.notes:
# Chemical Kinetics

> Rate laws, reaction order and the Arrhenius equation — how fast and why.

## Rate laws

The rate law relates reaction rate to reactant concentrations raised to their orders (found by experiment, not from the equation). Order reveals the mechanism.

## Arrhenius

Rate constants rise with temperature and fall with activation energy (Arrhenius). Taking logs turns this into a straight line — reusing logarithms from maths.

## What you should be able to do

- Write and use rate laws
- Determine reaction order
- Apply the Arrhenius relationship

chemistry.A1.chemical-thermodynamics.subject: chemistry
chemistry.A1.chemical-thermodynamics.title: Chemical Thermodynamics
chemistry.A1.chemical-thermodynamics.summary: Enthalpy, entropy and Gibbs free energy — predicting whether reactions happen.
chemistry.A1.chemical-thermodynamics.notes:
# Chemical Thermodynamics

> Enthalpy, entropy and Gibbs free energy — predicting whether reactions happen.

## Enthalpy and entropy

Enthalpy (ΔH) tracks heat; entropy (ΔS) tracks disorder. Reactions are favoured by releasing energy and increasing disorder.

## Gibbs free energy

ΔG = ΔH − TΔS decides spontaneity: negative ΔG means the reaction proceeds. This unifies energy and disorder, sharing a spine with physics thermodynamics.

## What you should be able to do

- Use enthalpy and entropy
- Apply Gibbs free energy
- Predict spontaneity

---

chemistry.A1.electrochemistry.notes:
# Electrochemistry

> Galvanic and electrolytic cells, the Nernst equation, and electrolysis.

## Cells from redox

A galvanic cell turns a spontaneous redox reaction into electricity; oxidation at the anode, reduction at the cathode. Cell voltage comes from electrode potentials.

## Electrolysis

Electrolytic cells use electricity to drive non-spontaneous reactions — extracting metals, plating. The amount deposited follows Faraday's laws (mole-charge ratios).

## What you should be able to do

- Describe galvanic and electrolytic cells
- Use standard electrode potentials
- Explain electrolysis

---

chemistry.A1.ionic-equilibrium.subject: chemistry
chemistry.A1.ionic-equilibrium.title: Ionic Equilibrium
chemistry.A1.ionic-equilibrium.summary: pH calculations, buffers, and the solubility product.
chemistry.A1.ionic-equilibrium.notes:
# Ionic Equilibrium

> pH calculations, buffers, and the solubility product.

## pH quantitatively

pH = −log[H⁺], so acidity is a logarithm of ion concentration. Strong acids fully dissociate; weak acids only partly, needing equilibrium methods.

## Buffers and Ksp

Buffers resist pH change using a weak acid and its salt. The solubility product Ksp governs how much of a sparingly soluble salt dissolves.

## What you should be able to do

- Calculate pH of acids/bases
- Explain buffers
- Use the solubility product Ksp

---

# Periodic Properties & s/p-Block

> Trends in atomic radius, ionisation energy and electronegativity, and s- and p-block chemistry.

## Periodic trends

Atomic radius decreases across a period and increases down a group; ionisation energy and electronegativity do the opposite. These follow from nuclear charge and shielding.

## Block chemistry

The s-block (reactive metals) and p-block (varied non-metals and metalloids) show patterns explained by their outer configurations.

## What you should be able to do

- Explain periodic trends
- Relate trends to electron structure
- Survey s- and p-block behaviour

Qualitative analysis identifies what is present (flame tests, precipitates); quantitative analysis measures how much (titration, gravimetry).

Good practical chemistry controls variables, repeats measurements and reports uncertainty — reusing the statistics and error skills from maths and physics.

> Transition metals, complex ions, ligands and colour.

d-block elements show variable oxidation states, form coloured compounds and act as catalysts — all traceable to their partly filled d-orbitals.

# Functional-Group Chemistry

> Alcohols, aldehydes, ketones, carboxylic acids and amines — reactions by group.

## Groups define reactivity

Each functional group has characteristic reactions: alcohols oxidise, acids neutralise bases, amines act as weak bases. Knowing the group predicts the chemistry.

## Interconversion

Functional groups convert into one another along known routes (e.g., alcohol → aldehyde → acid by oxidation), letting chemists build target molecules.

## What you should be able to do

- Recognise major functional groups
- Predict characteristic reactions

chemistry.F1.matter-particles-states.notes:
# Matter, Particles & States

> The particle model of matter, the three states, and changes of state.

## Everything is particles

All matter is made of tiny particles in constant motion. How close and how fast they move decides whether something is solid, liquid or gas.

## Changes of state

Heating gives particles energy to move apart (melting, boiling); cooling reverses it. Mass is conserved throughout — nothing is lost, only rearranged.

## What you should be able to do

- Describe matter using the particle model
- Explain the three states and changes between them
- Distinguish pure substances from mixtures

---

chemistry.F1.physical-chemical-change.subject: chemistry
chemistry.F1.physical-chemical-change.title: Physical vs Chemical Change
chemistry.F1.physical-chemical-change.summary: Telling physical from chemical changes, evidence of reaction, and conservation of mass.
outcomes: Identify signs of a chemical reaction
chemistry.F1.physical-chemical-change.notes:
# Physical vs Chemical Change

> Telling physical from chemical changes, evidence of reaction, and conservation of mass.

## Two kinds of change

A physical change alters form but not the substance (melting, dissolving). A chemical change makes new substances (burning, rusting), often signalled by colour change, gas, heat or a precipitate.

## Mass is conserved

In any chemical reaction, atoms are only rearranged — total mass before equals total mass after. This accounting principle underlies balancing equations later.

## What you should be able to do

- Distinguish physical and chemical changes
- Identify signs of a chemical reaction
- Apply conservation of mass

---

_A structured module in The Ultimate Learner — the essentials with all six learning layers. Deeper worked-example expansions are layered on over time; the three F1 "deep dive" topics show the target depth._
chemistry.F1.physical-chemical-change.mistakes:
# Common Mistakes — Physical vs Chemical Change

> Every learner hits these — spot them before they cost you.

- Calling dissolving a chemical change (it is physical).

- Assuming mass is lost when gas escapes (it left as a product).

- Missing subtle signs of reaction like a temperature change.
chemistry.F1.physical-chemical-change.tricks:
# Tricks & Problem-Solving Techniques — Physical vs Chemical Change

> Faster, cleaner ways to handle this topic.

- New substance formed? → chemical. Same substance, new form? → physical.

- Look for gas, colour change, heat/light, or a precipitate as reaction clues.

- Total mass is unchanged — account for gases too.
chemistry.F1.physical-chemical-change.memoryAids:
# Memory & Retention Aids — Physical vs Chemical Change

> How to remember this — and keep it.

- "New substance = chemical change."

- "Atoms rearrange, mass stays."

chemistry.F1.separation-techniques.notes:
# Separation Techniques

> Filtration, evaporation, distillation and chromatography — separating mixtures by physical properties.

## Separate by difference

Mixtures separate because their components differ — in particle size (filtration), boiling point (distillation) or how they travel through a medium (chromatography).

## Physical, not chemical

Separation techniques are physical: no new substance forms. Choosing the right one depends on the property that differs most.

## What you should be able to do

- Choose a separation method for a mixture
- Explain distillation and chromatography
- Relate method to particle properties

> Faster, cleaner ways to handle this topic.

- Filtration separates insoluble solids from liquids.

- Distillation separates by boiling point and recovers the liquid.

chemistry.F2.atomic-structure-i.subject: chemistry
chemistry.F2.atomic-structure-i.title: Atomic Structure I
chemistry.F2.atomic-structure-i.summary: Protons, neutrons and electrons; atomic number, mass number and isotopes.
outcomes: Use atomic number and mass number
chemistry.F2.atomic-structure-i.notes:
# Atomic Structure I

> Protons, neutrons and electrons; atomic number, mass number and isotopes.

## Inside the atom

Atoms have a nucleus of protons (positive) and neutrons (neutral), surrounded by electrons (negative). The atomic number (protons) defines the element.

## Isotopes

Atoms of the same element can have different numbers of neutrons — isotopes. They share chemistry but differ in mass, which explains non-whole atomic masses.

## What you should be able to do

- Describe subatomic particles
- Use atomic number and mass number
- Explain isotopes

---

_A structured module in The Ultimate Learner — the essentials with all six learning layers. Deeper worked-example expansions are layered on over time; the three F1 "deep dive" topics show the target depth._
chemistry.F2.atomic-structure-i.mistakes:
# Common Mistakes — Atomic Structure I

> Every learner hits these — spot them before they cost you.

- Confusing atomic number (protons) with mass number (protons + neutrons).

- Thinking isotopes are different elements.

- Forgetting neutral atoms have equal protons and electrons.
chemistry.F2.atomic-structure-i.tricks:
# Tricks & Problem-Solving Techniques — Atomic Structure I

> Faster, cleaner ways to handle this topic.

- Atomic number = protons = electrons (neutral atom).

- Neutrons = mass number − atomic number.

- Isotopes: same protons, different neutrons.
chemistry.F2.atomic-structure-i.memoryAids:
# Memory & Retention Aids — Atomic Structure I

> How to remember this — and keep it.

- "Protons define the element."

- "Neutrons = mass number − atomic number."

- Isotopes share chemistry, differ in mass.

1.prompt: An atom has 11 protons and 12 neutrons. Mass number?
1.explanation: Mass number = protons + neutrons = 11 + 12 = 23.

2.prompt: Two isotopes of an element differ in their number of:
2.explanation: Isotopes have the same protons but different neutrons.

chemistry.F2.chemical-formulae-equations.subject: chemistry
chemistry.F2.chemical-formulae-equations.title: Chemical Formulae & Equations
chemistry.F2.chemical-formulae-equations.summary: Writing formulae and balancing equations as conservation-of-mass accounting.
chemistry.F2.chemical-formulae-equations.notes:
# Chemical Formulae & Equations

> Writing formulae and balancing equations as conservation-of-mass accounting.

## Formulae

A formula shows which atoms and how many are combined, set by their combining power (valency). It is a compact recipe for a compound.

## Balancing

A balanced equation has equal atoms of each element on both sides — because atoms are conserved. Coefficients (not subscripts) are adjusted to balance.

## What you should be able to do

- Write formulae from valencies
- Balance chemical equations
- Interpret an equation quantitatively

---

_A structured module in The Ultimate Learner — the essentials with all six learning layers. Deeper worked-example expansions are layered on over time; the three F1 "deep dive" topics show the target depth._

- Forgetting a balanced equation must conserve every element.

- Miswriting formulae by ignoring valency.
chemistry.F2.chemical-formulae-equations.tricks:
# Tricks & Problem-Solving Techniques — Chemical Formulae & Equations

> Faster, cleaner ways to handle this topic.

- Balance by adjusting coefficients, never subscripts.

- Balance one element at a time, saving oxygen/hydrogen for last.

- Check every element's atom count on both sides.

> How to remember this — and keep it.

- "Balance coefficients, not subscripts."

- "Atoms in = atoms out."

- Formula = recipe set by valency.

2.explanation: Coefficients change amounts; subscripts would change the substance.

2.prompt: Balance H₂ + O₂ → H₂O. What coefficient goes in front of H₂O?

chemistry.F2.mole-concept.subject: chemistry
chemistry.F2.mole-concept.title: The Mole Concept
chemistry.F2.mole-concept.summary: The mole and molar mass — proportional reasoning applied to counting particles (the keystone topic).
outcomes: Define the mole and Avogadro's number
Convert between mass, moles and particles

CBSE: Cl.11 Some Basic Concepts of Chemistry

chemistry.F2.mole-concept.notes:
# The Mole Concept

> The mole and molar mass — proportional reasoning applied to counting particles (the keystone topic).

## Counting by weighing

A mole is a fixed number of particles (Avogadro's number, ~6.02×10²³). Because atoms are too small to count, we weigh them: molar mass (g/mol) links mass to number of particles.

## Ratios of particles

The mole turns particle counting into the same proportional reasoning as ratios: moles = mass ÷ molar mass. Every quantitative chemistry calculation flows from here.

## What you should be able to do

- Define the mole and Avogadro's number
- Convert between mass, moles and particles
- Use molar mass

---

_A structured module in The Ultimate Learner — the essentials with all six learning layers. Deeper worked-example expansions are layered on over time; the three F1 "deep dive" topics show the target depth._
chemistry.F2.mole-concept.mistakes:
# Common Mistakes — The Mole Concept

> Every learner hits these — spot them before they cost you.

- Confusing molar mass with atomic number.

- Forgetting to use the correct molar mass for a compound.

- Mixing up moles and grams.
chemistry.F2.mole-concept.tricks:
# Tricks & Problem-Solving Techniques — The Mole Concept

> Faster, cleaner ways to handle this topic.

- Moles = mass ÷ molar mass.

- Number of particles = moles × Avogadro's number.

- Molar mass of a compound = sum of its atoms' masses.
chemistry.F2.mole-concept.memoryAids:
# Memory & Retention Aids — The Mole Concept

> How to remember this — and keep it.

- "Moles = mass ÷ molar mass."

- "1 mole = 6.02×10²³ particles."

- The mole is ratio thinking for particles.

1.prompt: How many moles in 36 g of water (molar mass 18 g/mol)?
1.explanation: Moles = 36 ÷ 18 = 2 mol.

2.prompt: Mass of 0.5 mol of carbon (molar mass 12 g/mol)?
2.explanation: Mass = moles × molar mass = 0.5 × 12 = 6 g.

chemistry.F2.periodic-table.notes:
# The Periodic Table as a Map

> Periods and groups as patterns, not a list — organising elements by structure and properties.

## A map, not a list

Elements are arranged by increasing atomic number into periods (rows) and groups (columns). Elements in the same group have similar properties because they share outer-electron counts.

## Trends

Properties change predictably: reactivity, size and metallic character trend across periods and down groups. The table lets you predict, not memorise.

## What you should be able to do

- Read the periodic table's layout
- Relate group to properties
- Predict trends across periods and groups

---

chemistry.F2.stoichiometry-intro.subject: chemistry
chemistry.F2.stoichiometry-intro.title: Introductory Stoichiometry

CBSE: Cl.11 Some Basic Concepts of Chemistry

chemistry.F2.stoichiometry-intro.notes:
# Introductory Stoichiometry

> Mass-mole-mass calculations from balanced equations.

## Equations give ratios

A balanced equation's coefficients are mole ratios. They let you predict how much product forms from a given amount of reactant.

## Mass → mole → mole → mass

Convert reactant mass to moles, apply the mole ratio, then convert product moles back to mass. This chain is the core of quantitative chemistry.

## What you should be able to do

- Use mole ratios from equations
- Perform mass-to-mass calculations
- Identify limiting reactants (intro)

---

_A structured module in The Ultimate Learner — the essentials with all six learning layers. Deeper worked-example expansions are layered on over time; the three F1 "deep dive" topics show the target depth._
chemistry.F2.stoichiometry-intro.mistakes:
# Common Mistakes — Introductory Stoichiometry

> Every learner hits these — spot them before they cost you.

- Using mass ratios directly instead of mole ratios.

- Forgetting to balance the equation first.

- Skipping the conversion back to mass.
chemistry.F2.stoichiometry-intro.tricks:
# Tricks & Problem-Solving Techniques — Introductory Stoichiometry

> Faster, cleaner ways to handle this topic.

- Always balance first, then read mole ratios from coefficients.

- Mass → moles → (ratio) → moles → mass.

- The limiting reactant runs out first and caps the product.
chemistry.F2.stoichiometry-intro.memoryAids:
# Memory & Retention Aids — Introductory Stoichiometry

> How to remember this — and keep it.

- "Coefficients are mole ratios."

- "Mass → mole → mole → mass."

- Limiting reactant caps the yield.

2.prompt: In 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O, the mole ratio of H₂ to H₂O is:
2.explanation: Coefficients 2 and 2 give a 1:1 ratio.

3.prompt: The reactant that runs out first is called the:
3.explanation: It limits how much product can form.

chemistry.I1.acids-bases-salts.notes:
# Acids, Bases & Salts

> The pH scale, neutralisation, and an introduction to titration.

## Acids and bases

Acids release H⁺ ions, bases release OH⁻ (or accept H⁺). The pH scale (0–14) measures acidity; 7 is neutral.

## Neutralisation

Acid + base → salt + water. Titration uses this to find an unknown concentration by adding a known solution until neutral.

## What you should be able to do

- Describe acids and bases
- Use the pH scale
- Explain neutralisation and titration

---

> Faster, cleaner ways to handle this topic.

- pH < 7 acidic, = 7 neutral, > 7 basic.

- Acid + base → salt + water (neutralisation).

- Each pH unit is a ten-fold change in acidity.

chemistry.I1.bonding-i.subject: chemistry
chemistry.I1.bonding-i.title: Bonding I
chemistry.I1.bonding-i.summary: Ionic, covalent and metallic bonding, and electron-dot structures.
chemistry.I1.bonding-i.notes:
# Bonding I

> Ionic, covalent and metallic bonding, and electron-dot structures.

## Atoms bond for stable shells

Atoms gain, lose or share electrons to reach full outer shells. Metals + non-metals transfer electrons (ionic); non-metals share (covalent); metals pool electrons (metallic).

## Bonding sets properties

Ionic compounds form lattices with high melting points; covalent molecules are often low-melting; metals conduct because their electrons are free.

## What you should be able to do

- Distinguish ionic, covalent, metallic bonds
- Draw electron-dot structures
- Relate bonding to properties

---

_A structured module in The Ultimate Learner — the essentials with all six learning layers. Deeper worked-example expansions are layered on over time; the three F1 "deep dive" topics show the target depth._
chemistry.I1.bonding-i.mistakes:
# Common Mistakes — Bonding I

> Every learner hits these — spot them before they cost you.

- Thinking covalent bonds transfer electrons (they share).

- Confusing ionic and covalent based on name alone.

- Forgetting metals conduct due to delocalised electrons.
chemistry.I1.bonding-i.tricks:
# Tricks & Problem-Solving Techniques — Bonding I

> Faster, cleaner ways to handle this topic.

- Metal + non-metal → ionic; non-metal + non-metal → covalent.

- Count outer electrons to predict bonding.

- High melting point + conducts when molten → ionic.
chemistry.I1.bonding-i.memoryAids:
# Memory & Retention Aids — Bonding I

> How to remember this — and keep it.

- "Ionic transfers, covalent shares, metallic pools."

- "Full outer shell = stability."

- Bonding explains melting point and conductivity.

1.prompt: A bond formed by sharing electrons is:
1.explanation: Covalent bonds share electron pairs.

2.prompt: Sodium chloride (metal + non-metal) is held by ___ bonding.
2.explanation: Electron transfer between metal and non-metal is ionic.

chemistry.I1.rates-reaction.subject: chemistry
chemistry.I1.rates-reaction.title: Rates of Reaction
chemistry.I1.rates-reaction.summary: What speeds reactions up — concentration, temperature, surface area, catalysts — with rate graphs.
chemistry.I1.rates-reaction.notes:
# Rates of Reaction

> What speeds reactions up — concentration, temperature, surface area, catalysts — with rate graphs.

## Collision theory

Reactions happen when particles collide with enough energy. Anything that increases collision frequency or energy speeds the reaction: higher concentration, temperature, surface area, or a catalyst.

## Rate graphs

Plotting product formed vs time gives a curve whose slope is the rate — steep at first, levelling as reactants run out. This is rate-as-slope, shared with physics and calculus.

## What you should be able to do

- Identify factors affecting rate
- Interpret rate graphs
- Explain rate using collision theory

---

_A structured module in The Ultimate Learner — the essentials with all six learning layers. Deeper worked-example expansions are layered on over time; the three F1 "deep dive" topics show the target depth._
chemistry.I1.rates-reaction.mistakes:
# Common Mistakes — Rates of Reaction

> Every learner hits these — spot them before they cost you.

- Thinking a catalyst is used up (it is not).

- Confusing rate (speed) with yield (amount).

- Ignoring that rate falls as reactants deplete.
chemistry.I1.rates-reaction.tricks:
# Tricks & Problem-Solving Techniques — Rates of Reaction

> Faster, cleaner ways to handle this topic.

- More concentration/temperature/surface area → more collisions → faster.

- A catalyst lowers the activation energy without being consumed.

- Rate is the slope of the product-vs-time graph.
chemistry.I1.rates-reaction.memoryAids:
# Memory & Retention Aids — Rates of Reaction

> How to remember this — and keep it.

- "Faster = more or harder collisions."

- "Catalyst speeds up, stays unchanged."

- Rate = slope of the curve.

1.prompt: A catalyst speeds up a reaction by:
1.explanation: It provides a lower-energy pathway and is not used up.

2.prompt: Increasing temperature increases rate because particles collide:
2.explanation: Higher energy and frequency of successful collisions.

chemistry.I1.reactions-equations.title: Reactions & Equations Deepened

chemistry.I1.reactions-equations.notes:
# Reactions & Equations Deepened

> Reaction types, ionic equations and an introduction to redox.

## Types of reaction

Reactions fall into families: combination, decomposition, displacement, and double displacement. Recognising the type predicts the products.

## Redox intro

Oxidation is loss of electrons, reduction is gain (OIL RIG). Many reactions transfer electrons — the basis of batteries and corrosion.

## What you should be able to do

- Classify reaction types
- Write ionic equations
- Identify oxidation and reduction

---

chemistry.I1.solutions-concentration.title: Solutions & Concentration
chemistry.I1.solutions-concentration.summary: Molarity, dilution, and expressing concentration — the mole concept reused.
chemistry.I1.solutions-concentration.notes:
# Solutions & Concentration

> Molarity, dilution, and expressing concentration — the mole concept reused.

## Concentration

Molarity is moles of solute per litre of solution — again a rate/ratio. It links the mole concept to real solutions used in the lab.

## Dilution

Adding solvent lowers concentration but keeps the moles of solute fixed: C₁V₁ = C₂V₂. This is inverse proportion in action.

## What you should be able to do

- Calculate molarity
- Perform dilution calculations
- Relate concentration to moles

---

_A structured module in The Ultimate Learner — the essentials with all six learning layers. Deeper worked-example expansions are layered on over time; the three F1 "deep dive" topics show the target depth._

> Every learner hits these — spot them before they cost you.

- Confusing moles with molarity.

- Forgetting volume must be in litres for molarity.

- Thinking dilution changes the amount of solute (it does not).
chemistry.I1.solutions-concentration.tricks:
# Tricks & Problem-Solving Techniques — Solutions & Concentration

> Faster, cleaner ways to handle this topic.

- Molarity = moles ÷ litres.

- Dilution: C₁V₁ = C₂V₂ (moles conserved).

- Convert mL to L before computing molarity.
chemistry.I1.solutions-concentration.memoryAids:
# Memory & Retention Aids — Solutions & Concentration

> How to remember this — and keep it.

- "Molarity = moles per litre."

- "C₁V₁ = C₂V₂."

chemistry.I2.atomic-structure-ii.subject: chemistry
chemistry.I2.atomic-structure-ii.title: Atomic Structure II
chemistry.I2.atomic-structure-ii.summary: Electron configuration and quantum shells, treated intuitively.
outcomes: Relate configuration to the periodic table
chemistry.I2.atomic-structure-ii.notes:
# Atomic Structure II

> Electron configuration and quantum shells, treated intuitively.

## Electrons in shells

Electrons occupy energy levels (shells and subshells). Filling them in order of energy explains the periodic table's shape and each element's chemistry.

## Configuration predicts chemistry

The outer-shell configuration determines how an element bonds. Elements in the same group share outer configurations — hence similar behaviour.

## What you should be able to do

- Write electron configurations
- Relate configuration to the periodic table
- Explain energy levels intuitively

---

# Common Mistakes — Atomic Structure II

> Every learner hits these — spot them before they cost you.

- Filling higher shells before lower ones are complete (follow energy order).

- Confusing shells with subshells.

- Forgetting outer electrons drive reactivity.
chemistry.I2.atomic-structure-ii.tricks:
# Tricks & Problem-Solving Techniques — Atomic Structure II

> Faster, cleaner ways to handle this topic.

- Fill lowest-energy levels first (aufbau idea).

- Outer-electron count = group behaviour.

- Noble gases have full outer shells — hence unreactive.

# Memory & Retention Aids — Atomic Structure II

> How to remember this — and keep it.

- "Fill low energy first."

- "Outer electrons = chemistry."

- Full shell = stable/unreactive.

chemistry.I2.bonding-ii.subject: chemistry
chemistry.I2.bonding-ii.title: Bonding II
chemistry.I2.bonding-ii.summary: Molecular shapes (VSEPR), polarity, and intermolecular forces.
chemistry.I2.bonding-ii.notes:
# Bonding II

> Molecular shapes (VSEPR), polarity, and intermolecular forces.

## Shape from repulsion

Electron pairs around an atom repel and spread out as far as possible (VSEPR), setting the molecule's shape — linear, bent, tetrahedral, etc.

## Polarity and forces

Unequal sharing makes bonds polar; molecular shape decides if the whole molecule is polar. Intermolecular forces (including hydrogen bonding) explain boiling points and solubility.

## What you should be able to do

- Predict shapes with VSEPR
- Determine molecular polarity
- Explain intermolecular forces

---

_A structured module in The Ultimate Learner — the essentials with all six learning layers. Deeper worked-example expansions are layered on over time; the three F1 "deep dive" topics show the target depth._
chemistry.I2.bonding-ii.mistakes:
# Common Mistakes — Bonding II

> Every learner hits these — spot them before they cost you.

- Confusing bond polarity with overall molecular polarity.

- Ignoring lone pairs when predicting shape.

- Treating intermolecular forces as bonds within molecules.
chemistry.I2.bonding-ii.tricks:
# Tricks & Problem-Solving Techniques — Bonding II

> Faster, cleaner ways to handle this topic.

- Electron pairs (including lone pairs) spread to minimise repulsion.

- Symmetric shapes can be non-polar even with polar bonds.

- Hydrogen bonding raises boiling points sharply (e.g., water).
chemistry.I2.bonding-ii.memoryAids:
# Memory & Retention Aids — Bonding II

> How to remember this — and keep it.

- "Electron pairs push apart" (VSEPR).

- "Shape decides overall polarity."

- Hydrogen bonds → high boiling points.

2.prompt: VSEPR predicts molecular shape based on:
2.explanation: Electron pairs arrange to minimise repulsion.

3.prompt: Water has a high boiling point mainly due to:
3.explanation: Strong hydrogen bonds between molecules.

chemistry.I2.energetics.subject: chemistry
chemistry.I2.energetics.title: Energetics (Thermochemistry)
chemistry.I2.energetics.summary: Exothermic and endothermic reactions, enthalpy, and an introduction to Hess's law.
chemistry.I2.energetics.notes:
# Energetics (Thermochemistry)

> Exothermic and endothermic reactions, enthalpy, and an introduction to Hess's law.

## Energy in reactions

Reactions release energy (exothermic, ΔH negative) or absorb it (endothermic, ΔH positive). Bond breaking costs energy; bond making releases it.

## Hess's law

The total enthalpy change is the same regardless of the route taken — because energy is conserved. This lets us add known steps to find unknown enthalpies.

## What you should be able to do

- Classify reactions as exo/endothermic
- Interpret enthalpy changes
- Apply Hess's law (intro)

# Quantitative Equilibrium (Introduction)

Reversible reactions reach a state where forward and backward rates are equal — concentrations stay constant though reactions continue. Nothing has stopped; it is balanced.

If you disturb an equilibrium (concentration, temperature, pressure), it shifts to oppose the change. This predicts how to push a reaction toward products.

# Recursion

> Thinking recursively, base cases, and recursion vs iteration.

## A function that calls itself

Recursion solves a problem by reducing it to a smaller version of itself, until a base case stops the recursion. It suits naturally nested problems (trees, factorials).

Without a base case, recursion never stops (stack overflow). Every recursion needs a shrinking input and a stopping condition.

## What you should be able to do

- Write recursive functions
- Identify base and recursive cases
- Compare recursion and iteration

cs.F1.python-variables-types-expressions.notes:
# Python: Variables, Types & Expressions

> **Your first real step as a builder.** This assumes you have *never coded*. By the end you'll be able to store data, combine it, and predict exactly what a program prints — the foundation every later program stands on. We go slow on the mental model because a *correct model now* prevents a hundred bugs later.

## 1. What a program is doing

A program is a list of **instructions** the computer runs top to bottom. The most fundamental instruction is: *remember this value under this name, so I can use it later.* That's a **variable**.

## 2. Variables: a name bound to a value

```python
score = 10
```

Read this right-to-left: "take the value `10`, and bind the name `score` to it." The `=` is **assignment**, not equality (it does *not* mean "score equals 10 forever" the way maths does — it means "make score refer to 10 *now*").

**The box model (intuition):** picture `score` as a labelled box holding `10`. When you later write `score`, Python looks in the box and uses what's there.

```python
score = 10
score = score + 5     # take what's in the box (10), add 5, put 15 back
print(score)          # 15
```

That middle line confuses every beginner because it looks like the false maths statement "score = score + 5." It isn't maths — it's an instruction: *compute the right side using the current value, then rebind the name.* Right side first, always.

**Naming rules & good style:**
- Letters, digits, underscores; can't start with a digit; case-sensitive (`Score` ≠ `score`).
- Use meaningful `snake_case` names: `total_price`, not `x` or `tp`. Code is read far more than written; names are messages to the next reader (often future you).

## 3. The core data types

Every value has a **type** that determines what you can do with it. The four you need now:

| Type | Name | Examples | Represents |
|---|---|---|---|
| `int` | integer | `0`, `42`, `-7` | whole numbers |
| `float` | floating-point | `3.14`, `-0.5`, `2.0` | numbers with a decimal part |
| `str` | string | `"hello"`, `'A'`, `"42"` | text (a sequence of characters) |
| `bool` | boolean | `True`, `False` | truth values |

Check a type with `type(x)`:
```python
print(type(42))        # <class 'int'>
print(type(3.14))      # <class 'float'>
print(type("42"))      # <class 'str'>   <- text, NOT the number 42
print(type(True))      # <class 'bool'>
```

**Crucial:** `"42"` (a string) and `42` (an int) are *different values of different types*. `"42"` is three-then... no — two characters of text; `42` is a number you can do arithmetic with. Confusing them is the #1 beginner bug (see Common Mistakes).

## 4. Expressions and how they're evaluated

An **expression** is anything that produces a value. Python evaluates it and hands back the result.

### Arithmetic (on numbers)
```python
7 + 3      # 10   addition
7 - 3      # 4    subtraction
7 * 3      # 21   multiplication
7 / 3      # 2.333...  TRUE division — ALWAYS gives a float
7 // 3     # 2    floor division — drops the fractional part
7 % 3      # 1    modulo — the REMAINDER (hugely useful later)
2 ** 3     # 8    exponent — 2 to the power 3
```

Two dividers matter: `/` always gives a float (`6 / 2` is `3.0`, not `3`), while `//` gives the whole-number part. `%` (remainder) seems obscure now but is everywhere later — checking even/odd (`n % 2 == 0`), wrapping around clocks, cycling through lists.

### Precedence (order of operations)
Same as maths — **PEMDAS**: Parentheses, Exponents, Multiplication/Division, Addition/Subtraction, left to right.
```python
2 + 3 * 4        # 14, not 20  (× before +)
(2 + 3) * 4      # 20          (parentheses first)
2 ** 3 ** 2      # 512, not 64 (** is right-associative: 2 ** (3 ** 2))
```
When in doubt, **add parentheses** — clarity beats cleverness.

### Strings have their own operators
```python
"foo" + "bar"    # "foobar"   + JOINS strings (concatenation)
"ab" * 3         # "ababab"   * REPEATS a string
"foo" + 42       # ERROR: can't add str and int
```
`+` means "add" for numbers but "join" for strings — the operator's meaning depends on the *types* of its operands. And you can't mix: `"foo" + 42` raises a `TypeError`.

### Comparison expressions → booleans
```python
5 > 3      # True
5 == 5     # True     (== is "equal?", = is "assign")
5 != 3     # True     (!= is "not equal")
3 >= 4     # False
```
Note `==` (a **question**: are these equal?) vs `=` (a **command**: bind this name). Mixing them is a classic bug.

### Boolean expressions → combine truths
```python
True and False   # False  (both must be true)
True or False    # True   (at least one true)
not True         # False
(5 > 3) and (2 < 1)   # False
```
These power every decision a program makes (next topic: conditionals).

## 5. Type conversion (casting) — on purpose, not by accident

You often need to change a value's type deliberately:
```python
int("42")      # 42     text -> integer
str(42)        # "42"   integer -> text
float("3.14")  # 3.14   text -> float
int(3.9)       # 3      float -> int (truncates toward zero, does NOT round)
```
This matters most with **input**: everything a user types comes in as a **string**, even if it looks like a number.
```python
age = input("Age? ")     # age is a STRING, e.g. "15"
age = int(age)           # now it's the number 15, ready for arithmetic
print(age + 1)           # 16   (without the int(), "15" + 1 would crash)
```

## 6. Tracing: the core skill

The single most valuable habit is **tracing** — stepping through code line by line, tracking each variable's value, to predict the output *before running it*. Do it on paper.

```python
a = 4
b = a + 2        # a is 4 -> b is 6
a = a * 3        # a is now 12  (b is still 6 — b didn't change)
c = a - b        # 12 - 6 -> c is 6
print(a, b, c)   # 12 6 6
```
Reassigning `a` did **not** retroactively change `b`; `b` had already been computed from the *old* `a`. Tracing makes this obvious and trains the mental model that debugging depends on.

## 7. Reading a type error

When types clash, Python raises a **traceback**. Read it bottom-up:
```
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "prog.py", line 3, in <module>
    total = price + " rupees"
TypeError: unsupported operand type(s) for +: 'int' and 'str'
```
The **last line** names the problem: you tried `int + str`. The line above shows *where*. Fix: convert first — `str(price) + " rupees"`. Learning to read tracebacks now (rather than fearing them) is what separates people who get unstuck from people who don't.

## 8. Summary
- A variable is a **name bound to a value**; `=` assigns, right side first.
- Four core types: `int`, `float`, `str`, `bool` — and `"42"` ≠ `42`.
- Expressions produce values; know arithmetic operators (esp. `/` vs `//` vs `%`), precedence (PEMDAS), string `+`/`*`, comparisons, and booleans.
- Convert types **deliberately** with `int()`, `str()`, `float()`; `input()` always gives a string.
- **Trace** code by hand to predict output — the skill everything else builds on.
- Read tracebacks bottom-up; the last line is the diagnosis.
cs.F1.python-variables-types-expressions.mistakes:
# Common Mistakes — Python: Variables, Types & Expressions

### 1. Reading `=` as equality
Seeing `score = score + 5` and thinking "that's false, a thing can't equal itself plus 5."
> **Fix:** `=` is an *instruction*, not a maths equation. It means "evaluate the right side, then bind the name to that result." Right side first, then rebind.

### 2. Confusing `"42"` (string) with `42` (int)
`"5" + "3"` gives `"53"`, not `8`; then surprise when arithmetic breaks.
> **Fix:** quotes mean **text**. `"42"` is characters; `42` is a number. Convert with `int("42")` before doing arithmetic.

### 3. Forgetting that `input()` returns a string
```python
age = input("Age? ")
print(age + 1)          # TypeError: can't add str and int
```
> **Fix:** wrap it: `age = int(input("Age? "))`. Everything typed by a user arrives as a string.

### 4. Mixing up `=` and `==`
Writing `if x = 5:` (assignment) when you mean `if x == 5:` (comparison).
> **Fix:** `=` assigns (a command); `==` asks "equal?" (a question). In Python `if x = 5:` is even a syntax error — a helpful nudge.

### 5. Expecting `/` to give a whole number
`10 / 2` is `5.0` (a float), not `5`. Beginners expect an int.
> **Fix:** `/` is *true division* and always returns a float. Use `//` for floor (whole-number) division when you want an int-like result.

### 6. Misjudging operator precedence
`2 + 3 * 4` → expecting 20, getting 14.
> **Fix:** `*` and `/` bind tighter than `+` and `-` (PEMDAS). When unsure, add parentheses: `(2 + 3) * 4`.

### 7. Thinking reassigning one variable updates another
```python
a = 5
b = a
a = 10
print(b)      # 5, not 10
```
> **Fix:** `b = a` copied the *value* at that moment. Later changing `a` doesn't reach back and change `b`. Trace it line by line.

### 8. Trying to concatenate a string and a number with `+`
`"Total: " + 50` → `TypeError`.
> **Fix:** convert the number: `"Total: " + str(50)`, or use an f-string: `f"Total: {50}"`.

### 9. Assuming `int()` rounds
`int(3.9)` is `3`, not `4`.
> **Fix:** `int()` **truncates** toward zero (chops the decimal). Use `round(3.9)` if you actually want rounding.

### 10. Fearing tracebacks instead of reading them
Panicking at red error text and guessing randomly.
> **Fix:** read the traceback **bottom-up**: the last line is the error type + message (the diagnosis); the line above is where it happened. Tracebacks are the program *telling you the fix*.

### 11. Invalid or misleading variable names
Starting a name with a digit (`2nd = 5` → error) or naming everything `x`, `data`, `temp`.
> **Fix:** names can't start with digits; more importantly, use descriptive `snake_case` (`second_score`) so code reads like prose.
cs.F1.python-variables-types-expressions.tricks:
# Tricks & Problem-Solving Techniques — Python: Variables, Types & Expressions

### 1. Trace on paper with a variable table
For any tricky snippet, draw a table with one column per variable and one row per line executed. Fill in values as you "run" it by hand. This turns confusing code into a mechanical checklist and is the foundation of all debugging.

| line | a | b | c |
|---|---|---|---|
| `a = 4` | 4 | — | — |
| `b = a + 2` | 4 | 6 | — |
| `a = a * 3` | 12 | 6 | — |

### 2. Use `type()` and `print()` as your microscope
When something behaves oddly, print the value **and** its type:
```python
print(x, type(x))
```
Nine times out of ten the bug is "I thought this was an int but it's a str." Seeing the type instantly reveals it.

### 3. f-strings beat `+` for mixing text and numbers
Instead of fragile `"Score: " + str(score)`, write:
```python
print(f"Score: {score}")
```
No manual `str()`, no `TypeError`, and it reads clearly. Anything in `{}` is evaluated and inserted.

### 4. `%` (modulo) is the even/odd and cycle tool
- `n % 2 == 0` → `n` is even; `== 1` → odd.
- `n % 10` → last digit of `n`.
- Modulo wraps things around (clocks, days of week, cycling list positions). Remember "modulo = remainder" and reach for it whenever you hear "every Nth" or "wrap around."

### 5. Convert `input()` immediately, in one line
Fold the cast into the input so you never forget:
```python
age = int(input("Age? "))
price = float(input("Price? "))
```
This kills the most common beginner bug (string-from-input) at the source.

### 6. Parenthesize when precedence is unclear
You lose nothing by writing `(a * b) + c` even when the parentheses are technically redundant. Clarity for the next reader (and fewer precedence bugs) is worth more than brevity.

### 7. Swap two variables the Pythonic way
```python
a, b = b, a      # swaps in one line, no temp variable needed
```
A neat demonstration that the right side is fully evaluated before assignment.

### 8. Predict-then-run to build intuition
Before running any snippet, write down what you *think* it prints. Then run it. Every mismatch is a gap in your mental model made visible — the fastest way to learn the language's real behaviour.

### 9. Keep a "gotchas" note
Jot each surprise (`/` gives float, `int()` truncates, `"5"+"3"="53"`) into a personal note. These few rules cause most early bugs; a glance at your list resolves them until they're automatic.

### 10. Name to explain, comment to justify
A good variable name (`remaining_lives`) removes the need for a comment. Save comments for *why* something non-obvious is done, not *what* the line does. This habit scales to every future project and to reading others' code.
cs.F1.python-variables-types-expressions.memoryAids:
# Memory & Retention Aids — Python: Variables, Types & Expressions

## Core anchors

- **"`=` is a command, `==` is a question."** Assign vs compare.
- **"A variable is a labelled box."** A name bound to a value; look inside to use it.
- **"Right side first."** In `a = a + 5`, compute the right, then rebind the name.
- **"Quotes mean text."** `"42"` is characters; `42` is a number. Different types.

## Mnemonics

- **PEMDAS** — Parentheses, Exponents, Multiply/Divide, Add/Subtract. Same as maths.
- **"Slash floats, double-slash floors."** `/` always gives a float; `//` drops the decimal.
- **"Input is always a string."** So `int(input(...))` before doing maths on it.
- **"int() chops, round() rounds."** `int(3.9)` → 3 (truncates); `round(3.9)` → 4.
- **"Read tracebacks bottom-up."** Last line = the diagnosis.
- **Four types = "I Fear Strong Bugs"** → **I**nt, **F**loat, **S**tr, **B**ool.

## Visualization

- **The box-and-label picture.** Each variable is a box with a name tag; assignment puts a value in the box, reading the name peeks inside. When you reassign, you replace the contents — other boxes are untouched (kills mistake #7).
- **The conveyor belt for expressions.** An expression feeds operands through operators (respecting precedence) and drops a single value off the end. `2 + 3 * 4` sends `3*4=12` first, then `2+12=14`.
- **The trace table.** Columns = variables, rows = lines. Physically writing values as you step through is the single best habit for predicting output and finding bugs.

## Spaced-repetition prompts
_(Resurfaced at 1 → 3 → 7 → 16 → 35 days. Predict before checking.)_

1. What does `print(7 // 2, 7 % 2)` output? (→ `3 1`)
2. What is `type("3.0")`? (→ `<class 'str'>`)
3. `x = 5; y = x; x = 9; print(y)` — what prints? (→ `5`)
4. Why does `int(input("n? ")) + 1` need the `int()`? (→ input() returns a string; can't add str + int)
5. Evaluate `2 + 3 * 4` and `(2 + 3) * 4`. (→ `14` and `20`)
6. What does `"ha" * 3` give? (→ `"hahaha"`)
7. Does `int(2.9)` give 2 or 3? (→ 2 — truncates)
8. Difference between `=` and `==`? (→ assign vs compare-equal)

## The one-line recall card
> **A variable is a labelled box (`=` assigns, right side first); values have types and `"42"` ≠ `42`; expressions follow PEMDAS; `/` floats and `//` floors and `%` is remainder; `input()` is always a string so cast it; trace on paper and read tracebacks bottom-up.**

1.prompt: What does the operator `=` do in `x = 7`?
choices: Binds the name x to the value 7
Creates a constant that can never change
1.explanation: `=` is assignment: it binds the name x to the value 7. Testing equality is `==`.

1.prompt: What is the type of the value `"42"`?
1.explanation: The quotes make it a string (str) — text, not the number 42.

1.prompt: What does `7 % 3` evaluate to?
1.explanation: `%` is modulo — the remainder of 7 ÷ 3, which is 1.

1.prompt: What does `2 + 3 * 4` evaluate to?
1.explanation: Multiplication binds tighter than addition (PEMDAS): 3*4 = 12, then 2 + 12 = 14.

1.prompt: What does `"ab" * 3` produce?
1.explanation: `*` repeats a string: "ab" three times = "ababab".

1.prompt: Which expression is a boolean (evaluates to True or False)?
1.explanation: `5 > 2` is a comparison, which evaluates to the boolean True.

2.prompt: What does `print(10 / 2)` output?
2.explanation: `/` is true division and always returns a float, so 10 / 2 is 5.0, not 5.

2.prompt: After `a = 5; b = a; a = 12`, what is the value of `b`?
2.explanation: `b = a` copied the value 5 at that moment. Reassigning a to 12 afterwards does not change b.

2.prompt: Why does `print(input("n? ") + 1)` cause a TypeError?
choices: input() returns a string, and you can't add a string and an int
2.explanation: input() always returns a string. Adding str + int raises TypeError. Fix: int(input("n? ")) + 1.

2.prompt: What does `int(3.9)` evaluate to?
2.explanation: int() truncates toward zero (chops the decimal), giving 3 — it does NOT round to 4.

2.prompt: Trace: `a = 4; b = a + 2; a = a * 3; c = a - b; print(c)`. What is printed?
2.explanation: b = 6; then a becomes 12; c = 12 - 6 = 6. b kept its earlier value of 6.

2.prompt: What does `(5 > 3) and (2 > 4)` evaluate to?
2.explanation: 5>3 is True, 2>4 is False; True and False is False (both must be true for `and`).

3.prompt: What does `print(2 ** 3 ** 2)` output?
3.explanation: `**` is right-associative, so it's 2 ** (3 ** 2) = 2 ** 9 = 512, not (2**3)**2 = 64.

3.prompt: What is the last digit of 2471, computed with a modulo expression `2471 % 10`?
3.explanation: n % 10 gives the last digit of n: 2471 % 10 = 1. A common, powerful use of modulo.

3.prompt: After `x, y = 3, 8` then `x, y = y, x`, what are x and y?
3.explanation: The right side (y, x) = (8, 3) is fully evaluated first, then assigned, so x=8, y=3. This is the Pythonic swap.

3.prompt: What does `print("Total: " + str(3 * 4))` output?
3.explanation: 3*4 = 12; str(12) = "12"; "Total: " + "12" = "Total: 12". The str() is required to join a number into text.

3.prompt: Trace: `n = 17; tens = n // 10; ones = n % 10; print(tens + ones)`. What is printed?
3.explanation: tens = 17 // 10 = 1; ones = 17 % 10 = 7; 1 + 7 = 8. Floor division and modulo together split a number into digits.

# Complexity Intuition (Big-O)

> Big-O as "how does work grow with input size" — using logarithms from maths.

## Growth, not seconds

Big-O describes how an algorithm's work grows with input size n: O(n) linear, O(n²) quadratic, O(log n) logarithmic. It predicts scalability, not exact time.

## Why it matters

An O(log n) search beats O(n) massively on big data — the difference between instant and unusable. This reuses logarithms from maths.

## What you should be able to do

- Explain Big-O notation
- Compare algorithm growth rates
- Estimate scalability

# Control Flow & Arrays in C

> Conditionals, loops and arrays in C, and how they differ from Python.

## Familiar logic, stricter syntax

C has if, for and while like Python, but with braces and semicolons, and no automatic bounds checking on arrays.

A C array is a fixed block of same-type elements. Unlike Python lists, it does not grow, and going out of bounds is undefined behaviour, not an error.

# Pointers & Memory

> The core C idea: addresses, dereferencing, and the stack.

## Pointers hold addresses

A pointer stores the memory address of a value. & gets an address; * dereferences it (reads the value there). This is the idea Python hid entirely.

Local variables live on the stack, which grows and shrinks as functions are called and return. Understanding it demystifies how programs use memory.

# Strings & Manual Memory Management in C

> C strings as character arrays, malloc/free, and why Python never needed them.

## Strings are char arrays

A C string is an array of characters ending in a null terminator (\0). There is no built-in string type like Python's.

## Manual memory

malloc requests memory; free returns it. Forgetting to free causes leaks; using freed memory causes bugs. Python's garbage collector did this for you.

## What you should be able to do

- Handle C strings
- Allocate and free memory
- Avoid memory leaks

# Paragraph Architecture

> Building coherent paragraphs: topic sentence, support and coherence.

## Paragraph structure

A paragraph makes one point: a topic sentence states it, supporting sentences develop it with evidence or detail, and a closing sentence rounds it off.

## Coherence

Linking words (however, therefore, for example) guide the reader through the logic. Coherent paragraphs are the building blocks of every essay.

## What you should be able to do

- Write a clear topic sentence
- Support it with details
- Achieve coherence and flow

# Reading for Meaning

> Finding the main idea, making inferences, and telling fact from opinion.

## Main idea and inference

Every text has a central point supported by details. Inference means reading between the lines — drawing conclusions the text implies but does not state outright.

## Fact vs opinion

Facts can be checked; opinions express a viewpoint. Separating them is the first step toward critical reading and, later, evaluating arguments.

## What you should be able to do

- Identify the main idea and supporting details
- Make inferences from a text
- Distinguish fact from opinion

## What you should be able to do

# Vocabulary by Roots

> Building vocabulary through Greek and Latin roots, prefixes and suffixes.

## Words have parts

Many English words are built from Greek/Latin roots plus prefixes and suffixes. Knowing "bio" (life) and "logy" (study) unlocks "biology" and dozens more — vocabulary that compounds.

## Inferring meaning

Faced with an unknown word, breaking it into known parts often reveals the meaning without a dictionary — a far more powerful strategy than memorising lists.

## What you should be able to do

- Decode words using roots and affixes
- Infer meaning of unfamiliar words
- Build word families

Metaphor, simile, personification and imagery carry meaning beyond the literal. Naming and interpreting them is the core of literary analysis.

## Tone and structure

Tone is the writer's attitude; structure is how a text is organised. Both shape how a reader feels and understands — details are chosen, not accidental.

- Explain how structure shapes meaning

> Clauses, punctuation for effect, and controlling active and passive voice.

## Punctuation as control

Commas, semicolons and dashes control pace and clarity. Used well, punctuation shapes how a sentence is read, not just whether it is "correct".

## Active vs passive

Active voice ("the dog chased the ball") is usually clearer and more direct; passive ("the ball was chased") suits when the doer is unknown or unimportant.

## What you should be able to do

- Use clauses to vary sentences
- Punctuate for effect
- Choose active or passive voice deliberately

# Summarising & Paraphrasing

> Compressing and restating ideas precisely — a skill that serves every subject.

## Precise compression

A summary captures the key ideas of a text in far fewer words. Doing it well means separating the essential from the incidental — the same skill as taking good notes in science.

## Paraphrasing

Paraphrasing restates an idea in your own words at similar length, preserving meaning. It shows understanding and avoids plagiarism.

## What you should be able to do

- Write accurate summaries
- Paraphrase without changing meaning
- Distinguish summary from paraphrase

An argument makes a claim, backs it with evidence, and connects the two with a warrant (the reasoning). Naming these parts lets you analyse any argument.

- Evaluate whether evidence supports a claim

# The Persuasive / Argumentative Essay

> Writing an essay that argues a position with evidence and reasoning.

## Arguable thesis

A persuasive essay takes a clear, arguable position — one a reasonable person could dispute — and defends it with evidence and logic.

## Building the case

Each paragraph advances one reason, supported and explained. The strongest essays anticipate the reader's doubts (setting up counterargument, next).

## What you should be able to do

- Build a persuasive thesis
- Support with evidence and reasoning
- Structure a convincing argument

# Argument II

> Counterargument, rebuttal and spotting logical fallacies.

## Counterargument and rebuttal

A strong argument acknowledges the other side (counterargument) and answers it (rebuttal). This makes a case more, not less, convincing.

## Fallacies

Fallacies are flawed reasoning patterns (ad hominem, straw man, false dilemma). Spotting them protects you from bad arguments and strengthens your own.

## What you should be able to do

- Address counterarguments
- Write effective rebuttals
- Identify common fallacies

math.A1.calculus-limits-differentiation.notes:
# Calculus: Limits & Differentiation

> Limits made precise, the rules of differentiation, and applications like optimisation and related rates.

## Limits underpin calculus

A limit describes what a function approaches near a point, even where it is undefined. The derivative is formally a limit of average rates.

## Differentiation rules

The product, quotient and chain rules extend the power rule to any combination. The chain rule — differentiate outer, times derivative of inner — is the workhorse for composite functions.

## What you should be able to do

- Evaluate limits
- Differentiate using product, quotient and chain rules
- Solve optimisation and related-rate problems

---

# Complex Numbers

> The imaginary unit, the complex plane, modulus-argument form and De Moivre's theorem.

## Extending the number line to a plane

Defining i with i² = −1 lets every polynomial have roots. Complex numbers live on the Argand plane, with a real and imaginary axis.

## Modulus and argument

A complex number has a modulus (distance from origin) and argument (angle). This polar view makes multiplication a rotation-and-scale, and powers easy via De Moivre.

## What you should be able to do

- Do arithmetic with complex numbers
- Plot them on the Argand plane
- Use modulus-argument form

# Integration Techniques & Applications

> Substitution and by-parts integration, definite integrals, and areas and volumes.

## Techniques

Substitution reverses the chain rule; integration by parts reverses the product rule. Recognising which to use is pattern recognition built by practice.

## Definite integrals and applications

A definite integral gives an exact accumulated total between limits — area under a curve, volume of revolution, total displacement. It turns "adding infinitely many pieces" into one number.

## What you should be able to do

- Integrate by substitution and by parts
- Evaluate definite integrals
- Find areas and volumes of revolution

# Vectors & 3-D Geometry

> Vector algebra, dot and cross products, and lines and planes in three dimensions — the shared spine with physics.

## Vectors carry direction

A vector has magnitude and direction; you add them tip-to-tail and scale them by numbers. This formalises the scalar/vector idea met in F1 motion.

## Dot and cross products

The dot product measures alignment (and gives work in physics); the cross product gives a perpendicular vector (and torque). 3-D lines and planes are built from vectors.

- Add, scale and resolve vectors
- Use the dot and cross products
- Describe lines and planes in 3-D

math.A2.conics.notes:
# Advanced Coordinate Geometry: Conics

> Parabolas, ellipses and hyperbolas as slices of a cone, with their equations and properties.

## One family, sliced differently

Circle, ellipse, parabola and hyperbola all arise as slices of a cone. Their standard equations share a structure, and eccentricity measures how "stretched" each is.

## Foci and applications

Each conic has focal points with reflective properties — parabolas focus parallel rays (satellite dishes), ellipses model planetary orbits.

## What you should be able to do

- Recognise conic equations
- Identify foci, axes and eccentricity
- Apply conics to real situations (orbits, reflectors)

A differential equation relates a quantity to its own rate of change. dy/dx = ky models anything growing in proportion to its size — populations, decay, cooling.

math.F1.algebra-generalized-arithmetic.notes:
# Algebra as Generalized Arithmetic

> Variables are just numbers whose value we have not fixed yet; algebra is arithmetic with letters standing in for numbers.

## A variable is a placeholder

A letter like x simply holds a number we do not yet know. Every rule of arithmetic still applies — algebra generalizes it so one statement covers all numbers at once.

## Like terms and the distributive law

Only terms with the same variable part combine: 3x + 2x = 5x, but 3x + 2 stays as is. The distributive law a(b + c) = ab + ac is the engine for expanding and factoring.

## What you should be able to do

- Write and evaluate algebraic expressions
- Collect like terms and use the distributive law
- Translate word statements into expressions

math.F1.fractions-decimals.notes:
# Fractions & Decimals as One System

> Fractions, decimals and division are three views of the same idea — parts of a whole on the number line.

## A fraction is a division

The fraction a/b literally means a ÷ b. That is why 3/4 = 0.75 — dividing 3 by 4. Seeing fractions and decimals as the same number written two ways removes the sense that they are separate topics.

## Common denominators

You can only add or compare fractions once the pieces are the same size — a common denominator. Multiplying top and bottom by the same number renames a fraction without changing its value.

## Multiplying vs dividing

Multiplying fractions multiplies the parts (½ of ⅓ = ⅙). Dividing by a fraction multiplies by its reciprocal — "flip and multiply" — because dividing by ½ asks "how many halves fit?".

## What you should be able to do

- Convert freely between fractions and decimals
- Add, subtract, multiply and divide fractions
- Place fractions and decimals correctly on the number line

---

# Geometry I: Angles, Triangles & Congruence

> Angle relationships, triangle properties and the reasoning behind congruence — with construction, deferring formal proof.

## Angles that add up

Angles on a straight line sum to 180°, around a point to 360°, and the three angles of any triangle to 180°. These few facts unlock most elementary angle problems.

## Congruence conditions

Two triangles are congruent (identical in shape and size) if they match by SSS, SAS, ASA or RHS. Congruence is the basis of geometric reasoning — equal parts justify equal conclusions.

## What you should be able to do

- Use angle relationships (on a line, around a point, in a triangle)
- Classify triangles and use the angle-sum property
- Recognise congruent triangles by SSS, SAS, ASA

math.F1.number-sense-estimation.notes:
# Number Sense & Estimation

> Place value, negative numbers, orders of magnitude, mental math and the discipline of estimating before computing.

## The number line as one model

Every number — positive, negative, whole or decimal — lives at one point on the number line. Negatives are mirror images of positives across zero; adding moves right, subtracting moves left. Holding this single picture prevents most sign confusion.

## Estimation before calculation

Rounding each number to one significant figure gives a quick "ballpark" you can compare your exact answer against. If the exact answer is far from the estimate, you slipped a decimal or a sign — estimation is your error detector.

## Orders of magnitude

Thinking in powers of ten (is this in the tens, thousands, millions?) lets you reason about very large or small quantities without getting lost in digits.

## What you should be able to do

- Work fluently with negative numbers and place value
- Estimate answers using rounding and orders of magnitude
- Use mental-math strategies to compute quickly

---
