# Newton's Laws Deepened

> Friction, inclined planes and connected systems of bodies.

## Friction

Friction opposes relative motion and is proportional to the normal force (F ≤ μN). It converts kinetic energy to heat and must be added to force diagrams.

## Inclines and systems

On a slope, resolve weight into components along and perpendicular to the surface. For connected bodies, apply F = ma to each and to the system.

## What you should be able to do

- Include friction in force analysis
- Solve inclined-plane problems
- Analyse connected bodies

# Electricity II

> EMF and internal resistance, Kirchhoff's laws, and capacitors (introductory).

## Real sources

A real cell has internal resistance, so its terminal voltage drops under load. EMF is the total energy per charge; some is lost inside the source.

## Kirchhoff's laws

Charge conservation gives the junction (current) law; energy conservation gives the loop (voltage) law. Together they solve any circuit.

## What you should be able to do

- Apply Kirchhoff's laws
- Explain capacitor basics

physics.I2.kinematics-calculus.notes:
# Kinematics with Calculus

> Position, velocity and acceleration as derivatives and integrals — co-taught with calculus.

## Motion is calculus

Velocity is the derivative of position; acceleration is the derivative of velocity. Integrating reverses this. This makes the "slope = rate, area = distance" idea exact.

## Non-uniform acceleration

When acceleration varies, the SUVAT equations fail but calculus still works — integrate the actual acceleration function to get velocity and position.

## What you should be able to do

- Relate position, velocity, acceleration by calculus
- Differentiate/integrate motion functions
- Handle non-uniform acceleration

> Simple harmonic motion: restoring force, period, and energy exchange in oscillators.

## Restoring force

SHM happens when the restoring force is proportional to displacement and directed back to equilibrium (F = −kx). Springs and small-angle pendulums are examples.

## Period and energy

The period depends on the system (mass and stiffness), not the amplitude. Energy sloshes between kinetic and potential twice per cycle.

## What you should be able to do

- Describe energy in oscillation

physics.I2.thermal-physics.notes:
# Thermal Physics

> The gas laws and kinetic theory — a topic shared with chemistry, taught once.

## Gas laws

Pressure, volume and temperature of a gas are linked: PV/T is constant, giving the ideal gas equation PV = nRT. Each individual law (Boyle, Charles) is a special case.

## Kinetic theory

A gas is countless particles in random motion; temperature measures their average kinetic energy. This microscopic picture explains the macroscopic gas laws.

## What you should be able to do

- Apply the gas laws
- Relate temperature to particle motion
- Use the ideal gas equation

---

physics.I2.waves-ii.subject: physics
physics.I2.waves-ii.title: Waves II
physics.I2.waves-ii.summary: Superposition, standing waves, resonance and the Doppler effect.
physics.I2.waves-ii.notes:
# Waves II

> Superposition, standing waves, resonance and the Doppler effect.

## Superposition

When waves overlap, displacements add. This produces interference — constructive (in phase) or destructive (out of phase) — and standing waves on strings and in pipes.

## Doppler effect

Relative motion between source and observer shifts the observed frequency: approaching raises pitch, receding lowers it. It applies to sound and light.

## What you should be able to do

- Apply the principle of superposition
- Explain standing waves and resonance
- Describe the Doppler effect

---

_A structured module in The Ultimate Learner — the essentials with all six learning layers. Deeper worked-example expansions are layered on over time; the three F1 "deep dive" topics show the target depth._
physics.I2.waves-ii.mistakes:
# Common Mistakes — Waves II

> Every learner hits these — spot them before they cost you.

- Thinking overlapping waves collide rather than add.

- Confusing nodes (no motion) with antinodes (max motion).
